title: Right Speech
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up right speech, the third item on the Eightfold Path, and starts with how holding someone below or above ourselves bends what we say, using Nomon's own struggle to support a person who bristles at Nomon's advice. Nomon turns to the Zen precepts on praising oneself and denigrating others, then to the Buddha's three questions of true, beneficial, and well timed, and the ten-step checklist for correcting someone. Gil Fronsdal's Steps to Liberation invites curiosity about our own bad speech. Tonan O'Connor tells of exploding at her two sons in 1969 and coming home to three balloons, three bottles of Coke, and a note reading "We love you all the time." The evening closes with groups of three sharing a difficult communication.
topics: mindfulness of bodily action and speech
the importance of right speech in Buddhist tradition.

I think the biggest thing about these lists that is tricky is that we are so used to the way we are that these all sound like good ideas to be mindful about how we speak and what our intentions are and pay attention to what our views are and blah, blah, blah.

We all think that way.

Times when there is a lot of suffering and confusion are often rich times; you can catch yourself a lot.

One of the ways that we can get a little bit in trouble is a certain way we talk to people that we think are like sort of like a little below us, you know what I mean?
We are all nice people and we do not want to think badly of anybody, but so-and-so really could get it together, right?
It is true, right?
That is a view.
This really affects, I think, speech, how we hold a person.
Do we hold the person in a position below us or likewise above us?

Our speech is sometimes a little weird when we hold somebody above us; we do not say what we mean exactly and we are dancing around the point in some way, for all kinds of complex psychological reasons.
I think about this especially because I have been trying to support somebody who has really been struggling.
On the one hand, this person does really seem to look to me and really wants to know what I think and what I have to say.

I think, oh, she has a lot to learn, she has things to heal from, she is this, she is that, you know?
I am not really treating her as a full person in a certain way.
It is embarrassing to admit, but I think that is actually true.
I mean, you know, it is subtle.

Of the ten precepts, three of them have to do with speech.
One of them is honesty, which goes up probably in every ethical list as, you know, do not lie, be honest.

One is about not praising yourself, and one is about not denigrating others.
So our Zen ancestors were interested in this and noticed this all the way back to Buddha.
Buddha gave some general advice about wise speech or right speech.
The word right is a little problematic; maybe wholesome speech.
One of the short formulations he gave is one should speak only the words by which one would not torment or harm.
That word is well spoken if it does not torment or harm.

Is it actually true?
You know, are you sure?
We learned that great practice from Thich Nhat Hanh, right?
When you are thinking something about yourself or someone else, are you sure?
You know, check it out.

Maybe impossible, but as best you can tell, number one, is it true?
Are you sure?
Number two is, would it actually be beneficial to say this thing?

So not when the person is a mess, right?
When it is a good time for them to receive your words, when there is time to let it settle or.
I think that it is not just timing really either; it is like the whole situation, right?
Is it a beneficial, is it a good beneficial situation for somebody to hear something?
And often it is not, right?

A lot less.

We protect ourselves from wrong speech by having most of the time we are together be in silence, you know?

Number two, *am I one who practices purity in speech, flawless and untainted?* So I guess if you get off the pure speech train, you do not talk again in Buddhist orders, but I am not sure.
Is my regular speech good?
Am I a mindful speaker?

Goodwill, care a lot about everybody here, that is deeply in me.

Number four, it is a little bit longer: *Am I or am I not one who has heard much, who bears in mind what she has heard, who stores up what they have heard?

Do I really practice the teachings?
Do I really have them deeply in me?
And if I do not, maybe better not be giving anybody advice.
That is only four.
The fifth one is, are the rules of conduct, the precepts, thoroughly learned in my heart, well analyzed through knowledge of their meaning, and deeply practiced?
So is my conduct really good?
Do I know all the rules and guidelines for monastic life in this frame?
And do I practice them really well?
Then he says these five conditions must be investigated in oneself.

Consider the person that you want to straighten out.
And consider five more things.
It must have been pretty quiet if they followed these rules.
Do I speak at the right time or not?
Do I speak of facts or not?
Do I speak gently or harshly?
Do I speak profitable words or not?
Profitable is a weird translation, I think; beneficial is better.

So there is a lot of overlap with that first set of three here.
Is it the right time?
Is it true?
Is it beneficial?
